6.2 — Ground Checks: No Infinite Jumps

Your jump works. That is the problem. Tap the key in mid-air and you jump again, and again — a jump with no ground check is not a jump, it is a jetpack with infinite fuel. Today you give the script the one thing it has never had: a budget, and a way to refill it.

In this lesson you will be able to answer“why can I jump forever in mid-air?”Guided build
Break It Down~10 minGuided build

Your jump works anywhere, including in mid-air. The script is not wrong: it says if the key went down, add an impulse, and it does exactly that. What is missing is a rule about how often. So the whole feature is: give yourself a budget of jumps, spend one when you jump, and refill it when you land. Three small pieces, and the third is the one that makes the other two mean anything.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Give yourself a budget instead of a ruleTwo ints — how many jumps are left, and how many you are allowed between landings. One number cannot be both the limit and the count, and you need both before the limit can ever be changed.Read: the field declarations from 1.3
  2. Spend one when the key goes downThe jump condition from 6.1 with one term added, then jumpsRemaining -= 1 right after the jump. The gate decides; the decrement records. Both lines, in that order.Read: the jump you wrote in 6.1
  3. write this partRead: the trigger callbacks from 2.1, in their collision shape
  4. Say which surfaces count as groundThe Ground tag on the floor, and on anything else you want to be able to jump from. The cave has a second solid surface that carries no tag, so this is a decision about your level, not a line of code.Read: the tag-versus-collision distinction from 2.1
  5. Watch the number while you build, then take the instrument outA print() in Start() reports the budget you begin with. It is a tool for one afternoon, not a feature — the Console line it costs you every jump is not something a finished game owes anybody.Read: print() from 1.3

Four of the five parts are work you have already done: two ints are 1.3, the jump is 6.1, the callback is 2.1, and a tag is 2.1 again. The new idea is narrow and worth saying out loud — a limit is only a limit if something refills it. A counter that only ever goes down is not a jump limit, it is a countdown to standing still forever.

The test: could you look this part up on its own, right now, in one search? "Stop the infinite jump" cannot be looked up. "Do something when the player collides with the ground" can.

Your turn

Your budget is refilled by a message from the physics engine, not by asking a question every frame. Name one situation where the message arrives late, or does not arrive at all, and the player would tell you the game is broken.

maxJumps is 1. Before you change it to 2, say what else in this lesson would have to be true for a second jump to actually be a second jump.

In the Editor ~15 min
  1. Project window → open Assets/_Scenes/Platformer.unity, then Game view → press Play and keep tapping the jump key in mid-air. You climb, and the Console says nothing — your code is doing exactly what it says: if the key went down, add an impulse. There is no rule about where.
  2. Hierarchy → Grid → Collision, then Inspector → a TilemapCollider2D, a CompositeCollider2D and a Rigidbody2D whose Body Type is Static — which is why you land on it. Its Gravity Scale reads 1 and is greyed out, and both are correct: only a Dynamic body is moved by the engine, so there is nothing for that number to act on. Do not "fix" the 1 — switch this tilemap to Dynamic and the ground falls out of the level.
  3. Hierarchy → Grid → Collision → Inspector → Tag: it already reads Ground. Open Project Settings ▸ Tags and Layers and confirm it is in the list — the tag exists in this project, so nobody has to create it today. What you are checking is that the floor carries it.
  4. Hierarchy → Grid → Cave Exit → Inspector → Tag: Untagged, and solid, and carrying SceneSwitch.cs — touching it sends you back to the Overworld. Two surfaces you can stand on, one of which is not ground. Hold that thought for the trap below.
  5. Project window → Assets/Prefabs/Player, then Inspector → the Rigidbody2D (Dynamic, gravity on) and the BoxCollider2D you added back in 2.1 and 2.2. Those two are the reason the engine has anything to report to you at all — a callback is only sent to a body with a collider on it.
  6. Game view → play, land on the floor, then walk off a ledge and land on the cave mouth. When the walkthrough is done, one of those landings will give your jump back and the other will not.
The cave mouth is solid, and it is not ground. Cave Exit has the same three components as the floor and none of its tag, so landing on it does not refill your budget. Your code is working correctly and the player will still tell you the game is broken. That is the honest cost of a check built on a name: a tag answers "is this that one particular thing?", and every new surface has to be told the answer by hand. A later lesson comes back to this with a raycast and a layer, where the engine filters for you.

Socratic: Asking Versus Being Told

  1. Your budget is refilled by a message from the physics engine rather than by asking "am I on the ground?" every frame. Name one moment where the message arrives late, and what the player sees when it does.
  2. The cave mouth is solid but untagged, so landing on it does not give your jump back. Is that a bug in your script or in your level — and which one would you change first?
  3. maxJumps is 1 today. If you changed it to 2 right now, would you get a double jump? Name every line that would have to be true for the second jump to actually work.
In the Code ~20 min

There are three common ways to answer "am I standing on something?", and this project builds the first. Read all three — the differences are in when each one knows, and what it can tell you when it does.

TechniqueWhen it knowsWhat it can tell youWhere it lies to you
OnCollisionEnter2D() plus CompareTag() On the frame contact begins — a message from the engine. That you touched something, and what that something is named. Nothing fires when you leave, so the budget stays full until you land again; and every new surface needs the tag by hand.
OnTriggerEnter2D() on a small child under your feet On the frame the child's trigger overlaps something. That a particular point on your body is touching something. The child has to be placed by hand, and a trigger that starts inside a collider reports it forever.
Physics2D.Raycast() every frame Whenever you ask — every frame, for as long as you want. Whether something is under one exact point, how far away it is, and what it is. An infinitely thin line: a pixel of your foot over a ledge reports air. It also needs a LayerMask to filter what it may notice.

The third row is where this course goes next — 7.2 replaces the tag check with a raycast and a layer, which is what fixes the cave mouth without you tagging anything. Today is the honest first version, and it is what ships in most small games.

In the CodeGuided build

The question this answers“why can I jump forever in mid-air?”

You are editing Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs. Four small changes to the file you already have. Three are shapes from earlier in the course — two fields, a compound condition, a collision callback. One line is yours: the refill. Get it wrong and the jetpack comes back with no error message to explain why.

This build leaves 1 line for you to write. Everything around it is given, so you always know the shape of what you are producing.

Step 1Add the budget: how many, and how many left

Two lines in the class body, beside jumpForce from 6.1.

    int jumpsRemaining;
    int maxJumps = 1;
  1. 1How many jumps are left right now. No initializer: a field of type int starts at 0, and you are about to fill it in Start().Why not just start it at 1? Because a value that is set in two places (Start() and the landing) is a value you can forget to reset in one of them. Give it one source of truth — maxJumps — and set it from that everywhere.
  2. 2How many jumps you are allowed between landings. 1 is an ordinary jump. 2 is a double jump, and that is the whole of 6.4: one number changing.The limit lives in its own field, not in the condition. Written as jumpsRemaining >= 1 the 1 is hidden inside the gate; written as maxJumps the number has a name you can find, change and explain.

Step 2Fill it when the scene starts

In the else branch of Start() — the platformer branch you wrote in 6.1.

            jumpsRemaining = maxJumps;
            print(jumpsRemaining);
  1. 1One jump, on the floor, before you press anything. Without this line the game starts at 0, the first jump never fires, and nothing about the code looks wrong.This is the same sentence as the landing, said once at the beginning. A field that gets its value from another field is telling you where the real number lives.
  2. 2An instrument, not a feature. One line in the Console at the start of the cave, so you can see the budget you begin with. Delete it once the number is right — or leave it and be able to say why.Not a Debug.LogError(). This is not a failure; the game is working. A red line in the Console means "something is wrong", and spending that colour on a number you are watching trains you to ignore it.

Step 3Make the jump cost one

In Update(), the platformer branch — the else where linearVelocityX is set.

            if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.J) && jumpsRemaining >= 1)
            {
                Jump();
                jumpsRemaining -= 1;
            }
            rb.linearVelocityX = xVector;
  1. 1The jump from 6.1 with one term added. GetKeyDown is still what makes one press one jump; jumpsRemaining >= 1 is the new question — do I have any left? Read it in English before you trust it: "jump if the key went down this frame and I have a jump to spend.">= 1, not > 0. They mean the same thing here, and both are correct. Pick one and be able to say why: >= 1 reads as "at least one", which is what the player is thinking.
  2. 3The method from 6.1, unchanged. The force, the ForceMode2D.Impulse, the print inside it — none of it moves today.
  3. 4Spend it, inside the if. Inside is the whole point: a jump you were not allowed to take must not cost you one. Put this line above the if and a mid-air key press quietly drains a budget it never spent.-= 1 is jumpsRemaining = jumpsRemaining - 1. A shorter way to say the same thing, and it reads left to right as "take one away", which is what the player just did.
  4. 6Your horizontal movement from 6.1, untouched. It sits outside the if on purpose — you can always walk, whether or not you have a jump.

Step 4Refill it when you land — this is the blank

A new method, anywhere in the class beside Update(). This is the only line today with nothing earlier in the course to copy.

    void OnCollisionEnter2D(Collision2D other)
    {
        if (other.gameObject.CompareTag("Ground"))
        {
________________
        }
    }
  1. 1Not a trigger. The floor is solid and so is your collider, so the engine reports a collision, not a trigger — and the parameter is a Collision2D rather than a Collider2D. Same two callbacks you met in 2.1, in their solid shape.Enter, not Stay. This fires on the frame contact begins and then stops. Stay would fire every physics step you stood on the floor, which costs nothing here and would matter a lot if the body of this method ever did more than set one number.
  2. 3Only the ground. Everything solid is not ground: your cave has a second solid surface that carries no Ground tag, and this line is what makes that difference matter.
  3. Your turn5Put the budget back. One statement, using the two fields from step 1: the one you spend from gets the value of the one that sets the limit. Do not write a number here — if you write = 1 you have made maxJumps a lie, and the double jump in 6.4 will not work no matter what you set it to.The field that counts down is assigned the field that holds the maximum. Same line as the one you wrote in Start(), for the same reason — one source of truth for "how many you get".This line is what makes the other three mean something. Without it the player jumps once per scene and then walks. A budget with no refill is not a limit, it is a one-way door.
Check your work: the finished filetry every gap first — then open this to compare

Compare against your own file rather than copying it. The line that matters is the refill: jumpsRemaining = maxJumps — written from the field, never from a literal. The other three are the budget, the gate and the spend, and they do nothing useful without it.

// ------------------------------------------------------------------
//  REFERENCE FILE — Assets/Scripts/PlayerController.cs
//  Written to be read, not pasted. Build it with the walkthrough
//  above, one step at a time, then open this and compare.
//  If it is sitting in your project unchanged, that is the thing
//  to go and do now — the walkthrough is still above you.
// ------------------------------------------------------------------
using UnityEngine;
// ... plus UnityEngine.SceneManagement and System, from 6.1 and 3.5 ...

public class PlayerController : MonoBehaviour
{
    // ... speed, direction, animator, renderer, cooldownTimer, rb ...

    [SerializeField] float jumpForce;     // from 6.1 — the number you tuned
    bool isPlatformer = false;            // from 6.1 — set from the scene name

    int jumpsRemaining;                   // how many are left right now
    int maxJumps = 1;                     // how many you get between landings

    private void Start()
    {
        // ... the component lookups and the StatManager check ...

        Scene currentScene = SceneManager.GetActiveScene();
        if (currentScene.name == "Overworld")
        {
            rb.gravityScale = 0;
            isPlatformer = false;
        }
        else
        {
            rb.gravityScale = 1;
            isPlatformer = true;
            jumpsRemaining = maxJumps;    // you start on the floor
            print(jumpsRemaining);        // an instrument — delete when it is right
        }
    }

    private void Update()
    {
        // ... input, the facing block, the sword and the bullet ...

        if (!isPlatformer)
        {
            rb.linearVelocity = new Vector2(xVector, yVector);
        }
        else
        {
            if (Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.J) && jumpsRemaining >= 1)
            {
                Jump();
                jumpsRemaining -= 1;      // spend it only if you jumped
            }
            rb.linearVelocityX = xVector;
        }

        // ... cooldownTimer, the sword, the bullet, UpdateAnimation() ...
    }

    void OnCollisionEnter2D(Collision2D other)
    {
        if (other.gameObject.CompareTag("Ground"))
        {
            jumpsRemaining = maxJumps;    // landed: the budget is back
        }
    }

    void Jump()
    {
        print("jump");
        rb.AddForceY(jumpForce, ForceMode2D.Impulse);
    }
}
Build Lab: Prove It, Then Break It ~20 min

Step 1 — the four landings. Press Play and count your jumps in each: on the floor (one, then nothing), off a ledge and onto the floor (one again), onto the cave mouth (none — you found the trap), and in mid-air over nothing (none). If any of those is different, say which line disagreed with you before you change anything.

Step 2 — watch the number. Keep the print() in Start() for now and add one to the refill for a minute. Press Play and jump: the Console should read the budget going down by one on every jump, and back to the maximum on every landing. Take both prints out before you commit.

Step 3 — the spend that is in the wrong place. Move jumpsRemaining -= 1; above the if and play. You cannot jump at all: every key press spends a jump you never took. Put it back inside, and say out loud why the position is the whole difference.

Step 4 — the refill that is hard-coded. Change jumpsRemaining = maxJumps; to jumpsRemaining = 1;, then set maxJumps = 2 and play. You still only get one jump per landing. That is exactly the bug that would make 6.4 impossible, and it is a one-word fix.

Architectural specification: the budget.
  • Where does the number of allowed jumps live, and how many places read it? A limit written into a condition is a limit nobody can tune.
  • Is the spend inside the same condition as the jump? Say what the player experiences when it is not.
  • Which surfaces refill the budget, and how does the code know? Name the mechanism — a tag, a layer, a component — and one surface it gets wrong.

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Explain why a jump needs a budget rather than a rule
  • Say why maxJumps exists as a field and why the refill reads it instead of a literal
  • Explain why the decrement sits inside the if
  • Say what the engine reports when you land, and what it does not report when you leave
  • Point at the cave mouth and explain why it does not give your jump back
  • Commit and push
